title: Where AI belongs in a client workflow
metaTitle: Draft and sort. A person still sends.
excerpt: Use AI to draft, sort, and remind. Keep a person on any sentence a client will read as the studio's judgment. An automated line that is wrong is still your line.
alt: A white wall covered with framed prints, small plants, and two floating shelves. A wall someone edited, the way a studio should edit anything a model drafts.
caption: A wall that was chosen, not generated in a pile. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Where should a studio use AI in client work?
faqs.answer: Use it to draft a first pass someone will edit, to sort material into a pile a person can scan, and to remind the team about a record that already exists. Keep a person on recommendations, prices, dates, and anything the client will treat as the studio's judgment. The send button is the approval.

faqs.question: What should a workflow never send on its own?
faqs.answer: A price, a change in scope, a no, an apology, or a public line about the client's work. Those can start as drafts. They should not leave the building because a timer fired. Read the names, the numbers, and the promises before you send, because fluent text is good at mixing those up.

faqs.question: How do you tell if the automation helped?
faqs.answer: Ask whether a person replied sooner, whether the update had fewer missing facts, and whether anyone had to apologize for a sentence they did not mean. A count of prompts is not a result. If the tool only creates unread drafts, cut it back to draft, sort, and remind.

markdown:
AI automation for agencies belongs in the draft, the sort, and the reminder. A person stays on anything the client will read as the studio’s judgment: a recommendation, a price, a sentence about their brand, a design you are willing to ship. Automation that sends the wrong sentence is still your sentence. The client will not blame the tool.

Use a model to prepare the work. Use a person to send it. That split is the whole policy, and it should be written down where the team can find it on a busy afternoon.

## Draft, sort, and remind

Drafting is a first pass the author will edit. A project update from notes, a checklist pulled out of a long thread, a few subject lines for an email a person will rewrite. The draft is useful when it is faster to correct than to start from a blank page. It is not useful when someone sends it because the clock felt tight.

Sorting is filing. Tag a lead by the service they asked for. Group screenshots by page. Pull the open questions out of a kickoff transcript and list them. The output is a pile a person can scan. If the sort deletes mail or closes a task, a person should confirm the batch. Filing the wrong client into the wrong project is a quiet disaster.

Reminding is a nudge with a source. “The form from Tuesday has no reply.” “The domain renews next month.” “The staging link was promised today.” The reminder should link to the record and name the date. A reminder that only says “follow up” adds a notification without adding the fact.

Google’s guide to [creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) is written for the public web, and the standard travels. Content should be made for people, and it should be trustworthy. A client email is content under your name. An automated paragraph that sounds confident and was not read fails that standard inside the relationship, whether or not a search engine ever sees it.

## What a person still has to send

The client-facing line is short. If they will treat it as the studio’s judgment, a person writes it or approves it word for word.

- A recommendation about their brand, their site, or their product
- A price, a change in scope, or a date you intend to keep
- Anything that says no, or that explains a mistake
- Design, copy, or code you are presenting as ready
- A public case study, a caption, or a social post about their work

A person can use a draft for any of these. The send button is the approval. “I glanced at it” is not approval if you cannot repeat the claim. Read the names, the numbers, and the promises. Models mix those up with great fluency.

Internal notes can move faster. A teammate can receive a sorted list without a ceremony. Even then, do not let a model criticize a client in writing that might be forwarded. Tone in the internal channel becomes tone in the client channel the moment someone copies it.

If you would not sign the sentence in a Figma comment or in the repository, do not let a workflow sign it. Hanabi’s design work happens in Figma, Framer, and Illustrator, and the build is in the repo. The judgment lives in those artifacts and in the note a person attaches. A side tool does not get a signature of its own.

## Where the workflow may run

Attach the tool to a record you already trust. The project brief, the issue tracker, the form submissions, the shared folder. The model reads that material and returns a draft next to it. It should not reach into a personal inbox and improvise from whatever it finds.

Keep client material in the place you told the client it would live. Pasting a private strategy deck into a random chat box is a breach even if the output is pretty. Know which product you are using, what it stores, and who on the team is allowed to paste. If you cannot answer that, you are not ready to automate the draft.

Separate studios’ clients from each other. A prompt that includes one client’s numbers to answer another client’s question is a leak. Start a fresh thread per project. Name the project in the file so a person notices when they are in the wrong one.

Log what was sent to the client, by whom, and from which draft. You will need this the day a sentence is disputed. “The tool wrote it” is not a record. “Ada approved the update at 4 p.m.” is a record.

## Prompts are not a substitute for the brief

A good draft needs the same inputs a junior teammate would need. Who the reader is, what was already decided, what must not be promised, and the notes from the call. If those are missing, the model will fill the holes with plausible industry language. That language is how a careful studio starts to sound like everyone else, and how a specific client starts to feel unseen.

Write the constraints at the top of the prompt and leave them there. “Do not invent metrics. Do not offer a discount. Do not change the agreed launch page.” Then read the output against that list, not against your mood. The list is the review.

Refuse outputs that cite a fake source, a fake quote, or a fake law. Ask for the claim again with the source named, and if the source is not in the brief, delete the claim. This is the same discipline as the public site. Invented proof is worse than a shorter email.

Templates help for the sort and the reminder, where the shape is stable. They hurt for the recommendation, where the point is the specific client. Do not maintain twenty prompt templates for “strategy.” Maintain one policy and a few checklists.

## The failure you should rehearse

Assume the workflow will send the wrong name once. Design for that day. The send should be manual for client mail. The recipient field should be visible, not hidden in a zap that “usually” gets it right. A test client, or your own inbox, should be the first destination of any new automation. Run the real form through it. Read what arrives.

If a wrong sentence does go out, correct it yourself, quickly, without blaming the tool in the client’s inbox. Say what is true now. Then fix the step: add a confirmation, remove a permission, or stop the automation. A postmortem that only says “the AI hallucinated” will happen again next week.

Turn automations off when the project ends. A reminder that keeps emailing a former client is a defect. So is a bot that still drafts in a voice you retired after a rebrand. Put an end date on the workflow, or review a list of live ones every month. The list should fit on a page. If it does not, you have more automation than owners.

New teammates should see the policy on day one. What they may draft, what they must not send, which tool is approved. A ban you mention verbally will be broken by the person who joined after the meeting. Write it where the other studio notes live.

Keep a sample of a good draft and a bad one in that same note. The good one is a list of open questions pulled from a transcript, with no new promises added. The bad one is a client email that invents a date and a price. People learn the boundary faster from the pair than from a principle alone. When a draft looks like the bad sample, it does not get edited into shape in the outbox. It goes back to a person with the brief open.

If a client asks you to automate the replies themselves, show them the same boundary. You can sort their inbound and draft options. You should not let a workflow tell their customers something the client has not read. That request will come, because it sounds efficient. The sentence you need is the one you already use internally: a person sends anything the recipient will treat as judgment.

## Judgment stays billable

Clients hire a studio for taste and responsibility, not for a faster blank page. The time you save on sorting should show up as more attention on the work they will see. If automation only increases the volume of unread drafts, it did not help. Cut it back to the three jobs: draft, sort, remind.

Measure it plainly. Did the lead get a human reply sooner. Did the update go out with fewer missing facts. Did anyone have to apologize for a sentence they did not mean. Those are the results. A count of prompts is not a result.

The promise on a studio site is usually a response from a person. The system behind the form should make that response possible the same day, which is a different, simpler automation. [A lead form that notifies a person the same day](/blog/a-lead-form-that-notifies-a-person-the-same-day) is the next piece. It is about a ping a human will actually see, not about a model that answers in your place.

If you want to talk through which steps in a client workflow should stay human, [book an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the emails you send every week. The useful ones to automate are usually obvious once you say them out loud.
